articles.title: Your Database Has Backups. Have You Ever Tried Restoring One?
articles.description: Your backup job ran successfully last night.  This morning, a migration deleted the wrong data.  You...
articles.body_html:
Your backup job ran successfully last night.

This morning, a migration deleted the wrong data.

You open the backup dashboard. Everything is green.

Then someone asks:

“How long until the app works again?”

That’s when you discover whether you have a recovery process—or just backup files.

A successful backup is important. Restoring it and checking the application gives you much stronger evidence that you can recover.

Here’s a practical drill you can run before an incident makes it urgent.

1. Define what you need to recover

Start with a specific scenario:

“Our main database is unavailable. We need to restore the application using an existing backup.”

Write down two targets:

Recovery Time Objective (RTO): How long can the service be unavailable?

Recovery Point Objective (RPO): How much recent data can you afford to lose, measured in time?

For example:

Recovery time target: 60 minutes
Acceptable data-loss window: 15 minutes

These are examples, not universal recommendations. Choose targets based on what your users and business can tolerate.

AWS recommends performing recovery tests to validate whether your backup process meets these objectives.

2. Restore an existing backup into an isolated environment

Use a backup produced by your normal process. Creating a special export for the drill can hide problems in the process you actually depend on.

Restore into a separate database or environment with a clearly different name:

app_restore_drill

Check the destination before running restore commands.

Also isolate the recovered application from production integrations. You don’t want a test worker sending real invoices, emails, or payment requests.

Protect restored customer data with appropriate access controls, and remove the test environment when the exercise is complete.

Google Cloud’s recovery guidance recommends testing backups in a non-production environment.

3. Check whether you have everything the restore needs

Finding the backup file is only the beginning.

Can you access:

  • The backup storage account?
  • Required decryption keys?
  • Compatible database tooling?
  • Necessary extensions?
  • Database roles and permissions?
  • Application configuration?

For PostgreSQL, a single-database pg_dump does not include cluster-wide objects such as roles and tablespaces. Those need a separate recovery plan; PostgreSQL provides pg_dumpall for global objects.

This is exactly the kind of missing dependency a drill should reveal.

4. Inspect the restored data

A completed restore command doesn’t prove that you recovered the right data.

Check important business records:

  • Can you find a known customer?
  • Are their orders or invoices present?
  • Do payment totals match the expected state?
  • Are relationships between records intact?
  • Are permissions behaving correctly?

Compare against the backup’s expected recovery point. A backup from midnight won’t contain an order created at 9 a.m.

Use known transactions or recovery markers where possible. A single timestamp or total row count can miss problems.

Verify the data your application depends on, not merely the existence of its tables.

5. Start the application against the restored database

Now test the recovered application.

Can a test user sign in?

Can they open an existing record?

Can they create and update a new record?

Can the application generate an important report?

This can expose problems that database checks alone miss:

  • Missing permissions.
  • Unavailable extensions.
  • An incompatible application version.
  • Incorrect connection settings.
  • Missing files referenced by database records.

Your database might contain a document’s filename while the actual document lives in object storage.

Recovering the database is one part of recovering the service.

Check the other stateful dependencies your application needs.

6. Measure the whole recovery

Start the timer when you begin the recovery procedure.

Include time spent:

  1. Finding and accessing the backup.
  2. Preparing the environment.
  3. Restoring data.
  4. Configuring the application.
  5. Validating important workflows.

Stop when the service reaches your defined recovery criteria.

Record which incident stages the drill did not simulate, such as detection, escalation, or production traffic cutover.

You might discover:

Database restore: 12 minutes
Environment and application setup: 25 minutes
Validation: 18 minutes

Total drill time: 55 minutes

Reporting only the 12-minute restore would hide most of the work.

7. Measure the data-loss window honestly

Suppose an incident happens at 10 a.m., but the latest recoverable state is midnight.

That leaves a ten-hour gap.

A successful restore doesn’t make that gap acceptable.

If your target is 15 minutes, your backup strategy needs to support a sufficiently recent recovery point.

Depending on the database and platform, that may involve more frequent backups, transaction-log archiving, or point-in-time recovery.

Also distinguish the failure you’re testing:

  • If the database disappears, you want a recent recoverable state.
  • If a bad change corrupts data, you need a recoverable state before that change.

Newer isn’t always the correct recovery point.

8. Write instructions another person can follow

Document the process while you perform it.

Include:

  • Where backups are stored.
  • How authorized people obtain access.
  • Which tools and versions are required.
  • How to select the recovery point.
  • How to identify the restore destination.
  • How to validate the result.
  • Who makes the decision to return the service to users.

Keep credentials in your approved secret-management system, rather than copying them into the document.

Then have another team member follow the instructions.

If they need to ask you about several undocumented steps, you’ve found useful improvements.

A small recovery report

Your first report can be simple:

Scenario:
Main database unavailable.

Backup used:
Identifier and expected recovery point.

Restore destination:
Isolated drill environment.

Validation:
Sign-in, record lookup, create/update, reporting.

Measured recovery time:
55 minutes.

Observed recovery point:
Recorded and compared with the data-loss target.

Problems:
Missing role setup and outdated configuration instructions.

Follow-up:
Automate role provisioning and update the runbook.

Repeat the drill after fixing the gaps. Schedule future exercises according to the importance of the service and changes to its infrastructure.

Before your next deployment

Ask your team:

“When did we last restore a backup and run the application against it?”

If the answer is “never,” you’ve found a valuable engineering task.

Start small: restore one existing backup, validate one important workflow, and record what happened.

The first drill doesn’t need to be perfect. It needs to reveal what would otherwise surprise you during an incident.

Have you ever restored a backup that looked healthy but wasn’t enough to recover the application?

Further reading

  • AWS: Periodically recover data to verify backup integrity and processes
  • Google Cloud: Test recovery from data loss
  • PostgreSQL: Backup and restore

articles.title: My Harness Reported 0 Findings on 100 Files. All 100 Were Ignored.
articles.description: Three separate mechanisms make an ESLint run report zero while reading nothing — and every one of them exits 0 with an empty stderr. A clean bill of health and a file nobody opened are the same output.
articles.body_html:
I ran fourteen lint rules over 100 files and got back zero findings. Every
rule silent, clean sweep, nothing to fix.

The correct answer was 308 findings in 54 of those files. The harness had read
none of them, exited 0, and printed nothing to stderr.

Here are the three ways that happens, all of them measured this week, all of
them silent.

1. The files were outside the base path

ESLint resolves what it is allowed to lint relative to cwd. Point it at a
directory that is not under the cwd of the process, and every file comes back
ignored:

File ignored because outside of base path.

That string arrives as a message with a null ruleId — the same shape as a
parse error. If your loop counts messages.filter(m => m.ruleId), or skips
files whose messages look unfamiliar, you have just discarded the only
explanation you were given.

On the CLI it is quieter still. Exit code 0. Empty stderr.

Fix: set cwd to the tree you are measuring.

2. The .ts files were never eligible

Flat config (ESLint 9.39.2 here) matches files by pattern. Omit files, and
the default covers .js and friends — not .ts, in an ecosystem that is
mostly TypeScript.

// eslint.config.mjs
export default [{ rules: { "no-eval": "error" } }];

src/a.ts   ← contains eval()
src/b.js   ← clean

$ eslint .
$ echo $?
0

No output. Exit 0. The .ts file contains eval() and was never opened.

This one is worse than the first, because a partial corpus still produces
plausible numbers. A repository that is 80% TypeScript reports on the other
20% and calls it a result.

Fix: files: ['**/*.ts', '**/*.tsx'], explicitly, and check the count of files
actually linted against a count you obtained some other way.

3. The build under test was not the build you ship

In a monorepo, node_modules/<your-package> is usually a symlink into the
workspace. Anything you measure through it is unreleased source.

I asked a plugin which of its rules carry a fixer. From the workspace:

prefer-event-target: code

From the published package, same command, clean directory:

prefer-event-target: no fixer

Both true. Different questions. I nearly published a correction to a correct
article on the strength of the first one.

Fix: measure in a scratch directory with an npm i <pkg>@<exact-version>, and
say which tree the number came from.

Why all three survive review

Nothing throws. Nothing warns. The exit code is 0 in every case — and the one
time I saw a 1, it came from a real finding in a file that was linted, not
from the file that was skipped. "It exited non-zero, so it noticed" is the
wrong conclusion and I drew it once.

They also fail at three different layers — which files are eligible, which
eligible files are covered, and which build is under test — so fixing one
leaves the others exactly as they were.

And they all fail toward good news. There is no version of these bugs that
invents findings. That asymmetry is what makes them survive: a number that is
too high gets investigated, and a number that is too low gets celebrated.

The check

One rule, before you believe any of it: write the code the tool must flag,
and make sure it flags it.

export function C({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul style={{ color: "red" }}>
    {items.map((i) => <li key={i} onClick={() => log(i)}>{i}</li>)}
  </ul>;
}

Four lines, tripping at least two of the rules under test. If the canary is
silent, the corpus number is not a number.

That is what caught mine. The hundred-file zero was completely believable —
it was the four-line file reporting zero that was not.

A count from an instrument you have never seen fail is not a measurement, it is
a hope.

This is the cheap half of what ground truth catches that unit tests miss:
the tests all passed, because the harness they exercised was working — it was
the corpus it pointed at that was empty. It is also why a result you cannot
re-run is not yet a result, which is the whole distinction between
reproducibility and replicability.
And a zero that means "read nothing" corrupts the one cell every other metric
is derived from — the true-negative box of the confusion matrix.

Part of the Interlace ESLint ecosystem. Source on GitHub · Follow: Dev.to/ofri-peretz

What's the last clean report you got — and would you know if the tool had read nothing?

articles.title: pingpad: table tennis in the browser, with your phone as the paddle
articles.description: How pingpad turns a phone into a paddle over WebRTC: swing recognition on the phone, guiding the player between two devices, and Playwright tests for both.
articles.body_html:
pingpad is a table tennis game that runs in the browser. You open pingpad.app on a laptop, a tablet or a TV, scan the QR code with your phone, and the phone becomes your paddle. There's nothing to install and no account to create. You can play the computer, play a friend while the next players wait on the bench, or play alone and chase a record. Badges and records stay on your phone.

One of the people who tried it summed it up: "The Scan'n Play side of it works really well. No install, no questions, no pesky app store. I love it."

This article is about how it's built: a phone and a screen talking peer to peer, a swing recognised on the phone rather than tracked, a lot of work spent on guiding the player between two devices, and the library it all sits on.

It started with a counter

In 2019 I wrote a WebRTC proof of concept: a counter shown on one screen and driven from a phone. You snapped a QR code and updated the counter in real time. The goal was to go a bit further than the usual WebRTC exercises.

In 2022 it became webrtc-remote-control, an open source library for what any app runs into once a phone drives another screen: reconnections, page reloads, phones going to sleep, a remote that has to find its screen again. I had demos, the counter and an accelerometer moving a 3D object, and they worked. What I lacked was a game idea.

At the end of September 2026 I started on pingpad with AI coding agents. The library already handled the most critical part, the link between the phone and the screen, so I could build the game on top of it. The React and Vue bindings each come with an llm.md guide, written so that a coding assistant knows how to use them.

Five weeks later, pingpad has had over 200 pull requests merged.

Phone and screen, peer to peer

The phone and the screen talk over a WebRTC data channel. No game server sits between them.

Two devices still need someone to introduce them. I ported the PeerJS signaling server to Cloudflare Workers, on Durable Objects. It introduces the phone and the screen, then carries nothing. I picked Workers because the alternatives fit badly. Vercel cuts a WebSocket function after 300 seconds and bills its memory as long as the socket is open, so a screen left open would have used up the monthly quota in about a week. Render's free tier goes to sleep after 15 minutes. Cloudflare doesn't bill a hibernated Durable Object socket, so a screen waiting for players costs nothing.

STUN finds a direct path when one exists, even between a phone on 5G and a laptop on home Wi-Fi. Some networks make that impossible, such as a symmetric NAT or a corporate firewall. For those, Cloudflare's TURN relays the traffic, still DTLS-encrypted, so the relay can't read it. The screen shows whether each paddle connected over the local network, across the internet through STUN, or through the relay, something WebRTC usually hides.

On the same Wi-Fi, the median latency from phone to screen is 3.5 ms.

Recognise the swing, don't track the paddle

A phone can't tell where it is in space. Its sensors give acceleration and orientation, not position, so you can't track a paddle the way a camera would. What you can do is recognise a swing.

So the phone doesn't stream its sensors. It runs the swing detector itself, at full sensor rate, 60 times a second on iOS, and sends one compact, timestamped event when it sees a swing. The screen converts that timestamp with a clock offset it measures by pings, measured again regularly and from scratch when a paddle reconnects. Then the screen decides whether the swing hit the ball, by comparing the time of the swing with the time the ball reached the paddle. A network hiccup delays the message, but it doesn't change your shot.

I don't have a ping-pong table at home, so I recorded myself hitting foam stress balls with the back of the phone. A recorder on the phone captured each take, sensors and microphone together, and I labelled it: forehands, backhands, serves. The detector's thresholds come from those recordings, never from tuning by hand. A bench replays every recording through the detector. The detector is a pure module with no DOM dependency, so the exact same function runs on the phone and in the bench.

The microphone was there to hear the contact, and it showed that the acceleration peak doesn't mark it. Depending on how you swing, the peak can come before the ball touches the phone as well as after. That's why the screen decides the hit with a window around the ball's arrival, instead of trusting the peak.

I tuned the detector on an iPhone. It's meant to work on any recent phone, and it has played fine on Android too.

Guiding the player between two devices

A good share of the pull requests went into guiding the player, because this isn't a game where you tap your screen. You hold your phone like a paddle while the game plays on another screen, and nobody has that reflex yet. At each step, the player has to be told what to do, on the device they're looking at.

Some of the situations the game handles:

  • A visitor clicks Play on their phone, when the phone is meant to be the paddle. The game explains that this device would become the screen, and offers to send the link to a computer.
  • The QR code is scanned from Instagram's or Messenger's built-in browser, which won't give access to the motion sensors. The paddle says so, and how to open the page in the real browser.
  • iOS only grants the motion sensors after DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission(), called from a user gesture, on HTTPS. The paddle's button is that gesture.
  • Calibration shows a phone on the screen turning as the player turns theirs, so they can see what the game sees.
  • Once the ball is served, the paddle tells the player to watch the screen.
  • A phone locks, goes to the background or reloads mid-match. The game pauses instead of giving the point away, and the phone finds the game again when it comes back.
  • A third phone joins. It goes on the bench, in the order phones came in, and the screen calls it out by number. A player can hand over their seat, and a player who leaves keeps it until someone on the bench takes it.
  • A new version is deployed during a game. The protocol is versioned, so a phone and a screen on different versions notice it and say what to do.

Each of these has a message where the player is looking, phone or screen, and an end-to-end test that replays it.

Commands work the same everywhere. Pausing, choosing the match length or turning the sound off goes through one function on the screen, whether it comes from a button, a key, or a paddle. The screen sends each paddle the commands it offers, so any player can control the game from the phone in their hand. That was the point for TVs: once the game is open, nobody has to pick up the remote and steer a cursor through the TV's browser.

Testing a game that needs two devices

pingpad has 178 end-to-end tests, and 87 of them cover these player situations. Playwright opens the screen in one browser context and each paddle in another, emulating a phone, and sends the sensor events itself. A local PeerJS server starts with the tests.

Headless Chromium draws the 3D scene on the CPU. The screen and the paddles share that CPU, drawing the screen takes most of it, and the paddles fall behind. So in end-to-end runs, the screen doesn't draw, while its frame loop still advances the rally. The tests take less CPU and finish sooner.

The same fixtures film the demo videos for pull requests and the videos on the landing page. One setup drives the tests and the videos, so when the interface changes, the videos are filmed again with the same scenarios.

Those tests are what let me change the game without replaying every scenario by hand on two devices.

Working with agents

"A game in one prompt" makes for a good demo. pingpad wasn't one. What made agents useful on it was the setup around them:

  • the network layer was a library that already worked, documented for agents;
  • every change goes through a pull request, and every push runs format, lint, types, unit tests, build and end-to-end tests;
  • every pull request gets its own preview deployment, to try it on a real phone before it merges;
  • the dev server is reachable from a phone over HTTPS on the local network, thanks to portless, since iOS only gives motion sensors to a secure page;
  • a test that is written must fail when the condition it checks breaks;
  • an AGENTS.md file states the architecture and the rules, and the project records the decisions it lives with as ADRs;
  • every message between phone and screen is a schema, and the protocol is versioned, with each version frozen in a tested file.

I kept the design decisions, the tests on a real phone, and the approval of every merge. I wrote about how I work with AI agents on LinkedIn, in French.

What the game gave back to the library

Playing for real, with phones that lock, go to the background and change networks, turned up bugs the library's demos never showed. I fixed each one in the library rather than working around it in the game:

  • On iOS, a remote stayed listed after navigating away, because Safari skips beforeunload when it puts a page in the back/forward cache. The library now listens to pagehide (0.5.1).
  • A first connection whose ICE negotiation stalled waited forever (0.5.2).
  • Messages that arrived before the first listener was attached were lost, which affected the React bindings (0.5.3).
  • A page reloaded quickly could find its id still held by the signaling server (0.6.0).

The game's code is closed for now. webrtc-remote-control is open source under the MIT licence, with an llm.md guide for React and one for Vue: github.com/topheman/webrtc-remote-control.

Seven years after that counter, the phone has its game: pingpad.app.

I wrote this article with the help of an AI assistant, from my own notes and the project's history, and edited it myself.

articles.title: Clean Architecture in Angular: Is It Worth the Complexity?
articles.description: A practical exploration of architectural boundaries, dependency inversion, and the hidden cost of...
articles.body_html:
A practical exploration of architectural boundaries, dependency inversion, and the hidden cost of overengineering in modern Angular applications.

Clean Architecture is one of those architectural concepts that almost everyone agrees is valuable.

Until someone asks how many interfaces, abstractions, folders, and layers we actually need to implement it.

In backend development, separating business rules from infrastructure can make a lot of sense. But when we bring the same principles into Angular, things become more interesting.

Angular already provides components, services, dependency injection, routing, and a well-defined application structure.

So, do we really need Clean Architecture?

Or are we simply adding complexity to a framework that already solves many architectural problems?

Let's explore this question through a practical example. The code examples below are based on the companion Angular Clean Architecture Lab. Where the article shows a possible future HTTP integration, it is labeled as conceptual because the lab intentionally has no appointment API or HTTP repository.

1. The Problem: Angular Applications Don't Usually Start Complex

Most Angular applications start with something straightforward.

A component displays information, a service retrieves data, and everything works.

Here is a generic HTTP-backed service. It illustrates a common starting point; it is not the appointment service implemented in the lab:

import { HttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
import { inject, Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import type { Appointment, AppointmentDraft } from './appointment';

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class AppointmentApiService {
  private readonly http = inject(HttpClient);

  createAppointment(data: AppointmentDraft) {
    return this.http.post<Appointment>('/api/appointments', data);
  }
}

There is nothing inherently wrong with this implementation.

It is simple, readable, and easy to understand.

But applications evolve. We may add business validation, multiple API endpoints, data transformations, complex workflows, permission checks, state management, and error handling.

The important question isn't whether a service is too large. It is whether unrelated responsibilities are becoming coupled in ways that make future changes difficult.

2. What Clean Architecture Actually Tries to Solve

Clean Architecture is not fundamentally about creating folders named domain, application, and infrastructure.

Its central principle is the Dependency Rule: source-code dependencies should point toward inner policy. The Domain should not depend on Angular, HTTP clients, browser APIs, or persistence implementations. Application coordinates operations using inward-facing contracts.

A simplified view of this lab is:

Presentation -> Application -> Domain
Infrastructure -> Domain contract

Angular composition root -> Application and Infrastructure

The lab defines AppointmentRepository in Domain, so the Infrastructure adapter depends on that Domain contract. Other Clean Architecture designs can put a port in Application when its ownership belongs there; the important point is that the inner policy does not import an outer implementation.

The goal is to isolate business rules from implementation details. Changing a storage adapter should not require rewriting appointment rules.

Applying this principle does not mean every Angular application needs four layers. Architecture should solve an existing or reasonably anticipated problem, not introduce abstractions simply because they exist in a diagram.

3. Angular Already Provides Some Architectural Foundations

Before introducing additional layers, we should acknowledge what Angular already offers:

  • Dependency Injection.
  • Standalone components.
  • Services.
  • Routing and lazy loading.
  • Hierarchical providers.
  • Component lifecycle management.

These are valuable architectural tools. Angular Dependency Injection lets the composition root supply replaceable implementations. Standalone components make template dependencies explicit through their imports.

We do not need to recreate Angular's capabilities. Instead, we can define boundaries for concerns Angular does not decide for us: business rules, application operations, and domain-specific behavior.

4. A Practical Example: Vehicle Appointments

The lab manages vehicle appointments for a logistics operation. Its Domain currently enforces these rules:

  • A vehicle ID is required and is trimmed when the appointment is created.
  • The scheduled date must parse and cannot be in the past.
  • An active appointment for the same normalized vehicle and timestamp is rejected.
  • A cancelled appointment cannot be cancelled again.
  • Cancellation preserves the appointment record and changes its status.

The comparison page contains a conventional Angular service example. It uses the same Domain policies and repository adapter, but the service coordinates them directly rather than going through application use cases:

import { inject, Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import {
  isDuplicate,
  validateDraft,
  type AppointmentDraft,
} from '../appointments/domain/appointment';
import { APPOINTMENT_REPOSITORY } from '../appointments/infrastructure/providers/appointment.providers';

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class SimpleSchedulingService {
  private readonly repository = inject(APPOINTMENT_REPOSITORY);

  async create(draft: AppointmentDraft): Promise<string> {
    const errors = validateDraft(draft);
    if (errors.length) return 'errors.validation';

    const appointments = await this.repository.findAll();
    if (isDuplicate(appointments, draft)) return 'errors.duplicate';

    await this.repository.create(draft);
    return 'comparison.simpleSuccess';
  }
}

The returned strings are Transloco keys; localization belongs at the presentation edge. This service deliberately imports Domain policies and an Infrastructure token. It demonstrates a compact Angular approach, not the Clean Architecture dependency rule.

In a feature that uses a real backend, this simple service might call HttpClient directly. The lab does not include that backend, so its running comparison uses browser storage instead of pretending an API exists.

5. Introducing Clean Architecture

The Clean Architecture path in the lab separates the appointment operation from its storage implementation.

Step 1: Define the Domain

The actual appointment model uses ISO date strings, includes status and creation time, and represents a draft as a TypeScript interface:

export type AppointmentStatus = 'scheduled' | 'cancelled';

export interface AppointmentDraft {
  readonly vehicleId: string;
  readonly scheduledDate: string;
}

export interface Appointment extends AppointmentDraft {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly status: AppointmentStatus;
  readonly createdAt: string;
}

Validation returns typed policy errors without localized text:

export type AppointmentValidationError =
  | { readonly type: 'vehicle-required'; readonly field: 'vehicleId' }
  | { readonly type: 'date-invalid'; readonly field: 'scheduledDate' }
  | { readonly type: 'date-in-past'; readonly field: 'scheduledDate' }
  | { readonly type: 'already-cancelled' };

export function validateDraft(
  draft: AppointmentDraft,
  now = new Date(),
): AppointmentValidationError[] {
  const errors: AppointmentValidationError[] = [];
  if (!draft.vehicleId.trim()) errors.push({ type: 'vehicle-required', field: 'vehicleId' });

  const date = new Date(draft.scheduledDate);
  if (!draft.scheduledDate || Number.isNaN(date.getTime())) {
    errors.push({ type: 'date-invalid', field: 'scheduledDate' });
  } else if (date.getTime() < now.getTime()) {
    errors.push({ type: 'date-in-past', field: 'scheduledDate' });
  }

  return errors;
}

The Domain also owns duplicate detection and the cancellation transition. It imports TypeScript only. Transloco messages are selected by Presentation, keeping localization out of business policy.

Step 2: Define the Repository Contract

In this project the repository contract lives in Domain because it is expressed in terms of Domain appointments and drafts:

import type { Appointment, AppointmentDraft } from './appointment';

export interface AppointmentRepository {
  findAll(): Promise<Appointment[]>;
  findById(id: string): Promise<Appointment | null>;
  create(draft: AppointmentDraft): Promise<Appointment>;
  cancel(id: string): Promise<Appointment>;
}

The port exposes only operations required by the use cases. There is no generic update operation that could edit a cancelled appointment.

Step 3: Represent Expected Failures Explicitly

The lab uses a discriminated Result union:

export type Result<T, E> =
  { readonly success: true; readonly value: T } | { readonly success: false; readonly error: E };

Application errors distinguish validation, duplicate, not-found, already-cancelled, and expected infrastructure failures:

import type { AppointmentValidationError } from '../domain/appointment';

export type AppointmentError =
  | { readonly type: 'validation-failure'; readonly errors: AppointmentValidationError[] }
  | { readonly type: 'appointment-not-found'; readonly id: string }
  | { readonly type: 'duplicate-appointment' }
  | { readonly type: 'appointment-already-cancelled' }
  | { readonly type: 'infrastructure-failure'; readonly message: string };

Expected business failures are part of the use-case contract. Unexpected exceptions are not silently converted into business results. A Result type is one option for making expected outcomes explicit; Clean Architecture does not require this particular error style.

Step 4: Implement the Use Case

The following excerpt follows CreateAppointmentUseCase in the lab. It validates, checks duplicates, normalizes the draft, and translates only the adapter's known InfrastructureFailure. Other exceptions propagate:

async execute(draft: AppointmentDraft): Promise<Result<Appointment, AppointmentError>> {
  const errors = validateDraft(draft, this.clock());
  if (errors.length) return err({ type: 'validation-failure', errors });

  try {
    if (isDuplicate(await this.repository.findAll(), draft)) {
      return err({ type: 'duplicate-appointment' });
    }

    return ok(
      await this.repository.create({
        vehicleId: draft.vehicleId.trim(),
        scheduledDate: new Date(draft.scheduledDate).toISOString(),
      }),
    );
  } catch (cause) {
    if (cause instanceof InfrastructureFailure) {
      return err({ type: 'infrastructure-failure', message: cause.message });
    }
    throw cause;
  }
}

The use case does not know about Angular, HttpClient, or a storage key. Cancellation and read operations have their own use cases.

6. Implementing the Infrastructure Adapter

The actual adapter is InMemoryAppointmentRepository. Despite its name, it persists appointment JSON in browser localStorage and keeps an in-memory cache. It validates stored records and returns copies so callers do not mutate its stored objects.

The project has no appointment API, HTTP repository, API DTO, or mapper. HttpClient is configured for Transloco's same-origin language catalog files, not appointment persistence.

If an API is added later, an HTTP adapter can implement AppointmentRepository. Introduce API DTOs and mapping when the wire representation differs from the Domain model. This is an architectural extension point, not a currently demonstrated adapter replacement.

7. Connecting Dependencies with Angular DI

TypeScript interfaces do not exist at runtime, so Angular cannot inject AppointmentRepository directly. The project declares an InjectionToken:

import { InjectionToken } from '@angular/core';

export const APPOINTMENT_REPOSITORY = new InjectionToken<AppointmentRepository>(
  'APPOINTMENT_REPOSITORY',
);

Infrastructure provides its adapter under that token:

import { InMemoryAppointmentRepository } from '../repositories/in-memory-appointment.repository';
import type { AppointmentRepository } from '../../domain/appointment.repository';

export const appointmentProviders = [
  InMemoryAppointmentRepository,
  { provide: APPOINTMENT_REPOSITORY, useExisting: InMemoryAppointmentRepository },
];

The Angular composition root creates the use case from the token. This is the actual provider pattern used by the project:

{
  provide: CREATE_APPOINTMENT,
  useFactory: (repository: ConstructorParameters<typeof CreateAppointmentUseCase>[0]) =>
    new CreateAppointmentUseCase(repository),
  deps: [APPOINTMENT_REPOSITORY],
}

The facade injects the use-case token, while the use case remains a plain TypeScript class. The repository can also be replaced in tests through DI. A production HTTP implementation is possible, but it has not been added to this no-backend lab.

8. Testing the Use Case Without Angular

The application tests instantiate use cases directly and provide a FakeAppointmentRepository. The fake implements all four operations required by the real contract; there is no Angular TestBed in Domain or Application tests.

For example, the fake's create operation constructs the actual Domain shape:

async create(draft: AppointmentDraft): Promise<Appointment> {
  const item: Appointment = {
    ...draft,
    id: 'id-' + (this.records.length + 1),
    status: 'scheduled',
    createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  };
  this.records.push(item);
  return item;
}

A test uses a relative future date so it remains valid when run later:

const draft: AppointmentDraft = {
  vehicleId: 'TRK-9',
  scheduledDate: new Date(Date.now() + 86_400_000).toISOString(),
};

const result = await new CreateAppointmentUseCase(repository).execute(draft);

expect(result.success).toBe(true);
expect(repository.records).toHaveLength(1);

The full suite also tests invalid and duplicate creation, missing records, repeated cancellation, infrastructure failures, and unexpected exceptions. Infrastructure tests cover browser storage; Presentation tests use Angular TestBed. The layers use different test techniques because they have different responsibilities.

9. Comparing the Two Approaches

Aspect Conventional Angular service Clean Architecture path
Initial implementation Fewer files and direct orchestration More setup and indirection
Business rules Shared Domain functions called by the service Domain rules coordinated by an application use case
Persistence dependency Service injects the repository token directly Use case depends on the Domain repository contract
Unit testing business flow Possible, but the service has Angular and adapter dependencies Use case runs with a fake repository and no TestBed
HTTP replacement Not demonstrated by this lab A compatible adapter could be added behind the repository contract; no HTTP adapter exists today
Navigation through code Direct More layers and tokens to navigate
Good fit Small, stable flows Workflows or policies likely to evolve

The comparison is intentionally bounded: both paths use the same Domain policies and local storage, but the Clean path isolates orchestration behind a use case. It does not demonstrate an HTTP adapter swap. Neither approach is inherently superior; the appropriate trade-off depends on change and business-rule complexity.

10. The Hidden Cost of Clean Architecture

For this small workflow, the Clean path adds four use cases, repository and use-case tokens, provider wiring, a facade, and more files. These are real navigation and maintenance costs.

Boilerplate is not free

Every abstraction has a maintenance cost. Developers need to understand where behavior lives, how dependencies are wired, and which layer owns an operation.

Interfaces are not automatically valuable

An interface is useful when it defines a meaningful boundary. It is less useful when it only duplicates a stable implementation with no replacement or testing value. Dependency inversion is about controlling dependencies, not maximizing interfaces.

Abstraction can hide simple behavior

Excessive indirection can make an API request harder to trace. The goal is to make important behavior easier to change and understand, not harder to find.

11. When Is Clean Architecture Worth It?

There is no universal answer. These are heuristics, not rules:

Situation Possible choice
Small CRUD application with little policy Keep the service focused and simple
Prototype or short-lived project Avoid abstractions without a concrete need
Complex business workflows Consider application use cases
Domain with significant business rules Isolate the domain policy
Multiple entry points must share an operation Reusable application logic may help
Infrastructure changes are likely A repository boundary may reduce coupling

A small application can have complex business rules, and a large application can still be overengineered. The relevant measure is the cost of changing and understanding behavior, not the number of files.

12. A More Pragmatic Approach: Start with Boundaries, Not Layers

Instead of starting with a predefined folder structure, identify responsibilities that need separation. A complex feature might benefit from Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and Presentation folders. A small notification feature might need only a service and component.

Do not add all four folders to every feature automatically. A straightforward service with clear responsibilities can be easier to maintain than an elaborate structure that does not solve a real problem.

13. Final Thoughts

Clean Architecture isn't inherently too complex for Angular. The problem is applying patterns without understanding what they are meant to solve.

Angular provides many tools for maintainable applications. Clean Architecture can complement them by isolating business rules and controlling dependency direction, but every boundary adds complexity.

Don't adopt Clean Architecture because your project is large. Adopt its principles when your business complexity justifies them.

Start with the simplest architecture that solves the current problem. Introduce stronger boundaries when the cost of coupling becomes real. The best architecture is the one that makes the application easier to understand, change, and maintain.

What do you think?

Do you use Clean Architecture in your Angular applications? Have you found that it improves maintainability, or does it introduce more complexity than necessary?

I'd love to hear how other developers approach this trade-off.

articles.title: Rack Before You Remember
articles.description: What racking wine teaches about agent memory    The mead's lees on October 21, with the racking cane...
articles.body_html:
What racking wine teaches about agent memory

The mead's lees on October 21, with the racking cane at the edge. Everything the siphon left behind stays here.

That layer at the bottom of my mead fermenter did most of the work of turning honey and water into something worth drinking. It's spent yeast and the debris of a few weeks of vigorous fermentation. Without it, there'd be nothing to rack.

I left all of it behind on purpose.

What lees are, and why they stay behind

When primary fermentation winds down, the yeast that did the work drops out of suspension along with whatever solids came along for the ride. That sediment is called the lees, and the first, heaviest layer is known as the gross lees.

Racking is how you separate the wine from it. You siphon the wine off from above, carefully, into a clean vessel, and leave the sediment where it settled. I racked the pear wine on October 12, once the readings had held steady long enough to justify the move, and the mead on October 21, when its refractometer reading had settled at 3.2 Brix.

The pear racking went smoothly, and it taught me something I didn't expect. I'd added bentonite, a clay that binds proteins and helps haze drop out, and I assumed that by racking day the wine would be close to see-through. It wasn't. It's not murky, but it's not clear either. Racking had separated the wine from the heavy sediment. It hadn't made the wine clean. The finer material still in suspension will take weeks to settle, and there will be another racking after it does.

Hold on to that distinction, because it comes back later.

The reason to rack isn't that the lees are bad. It's that their job is done. Left in contact with the wine too long, the heavy lees start to break down, and the compounds they release can push the wine toward off flavors that range from dull to genuinely unpleasant. Material that was essential during fermentation becomes a liability during aging.

That's the whole article in one sentence: not everything useful during execution deserves to survive execution.

Agents have lees too

Watch an AI agent work through a nontrivial task and you'll see the equivalent of a primary fermentation. It retrieves documents, most of which turn out to be irrelevant. It calls tools and gets back large blobs of output. It tries an approach, hits an error, and backs out. It forms hypotheses that don't survive. It reads text from untrusted sources, some of which might contain instructions it was never supposed to follow.

All of that is essential while the task is running. The failed attempts are how it found the working one. The irrelevant documents are how it figured out which were relevant.

And then the task ends, and a surprising number of memory designs do the equivalent of never racking the wine. The transcript gets saved. The tool outputs get embedded. The scratchpad gets summarized into long-term memory without anyone deciding which parts of it were conclusions and which were sediment.

For a while, nothing seems wrong. Then the lees start to break down. A hypothesis the agent abandoned on Tuesday gets retrieved on Friday as if it were a fact. An error message from a transient outage becomes a durable belief that some service is broken. A snippet of injected text from a web page resurfaces, weeks later, in a context where it looks like a user preference. None of these were bad things to have during the task. They're bad things to have in the cellar.

You can't filter it out at the glass

The obvious objection is that you can sort it out later. Store everything, and let retrieval figure out what's relevant.

Winemaking has a pretty clear answer to that. If you leave the wine on the gross lees for months, you can't fix it by pouring carefully. The problem isn't that sediment ends up in the glass; you could decant that away. The problem is what the sediment did to the wine while it was stored together.

Memory systems work the same way. Raw execution material doesn't just sit inertly waiting to be filtered at read time. It gets summarized, and the summaries inherit its errors. It gets embedded, and it competes in similarity search with things that were actually true. It feeds derived facts, and those facts get cited by later tasks. By the time a read-side filter sees it, the contamination has already been folded into things that look clean.

None of this means throwing the raw record away. Transcripts and tool outputs are genuinely valuable for debugging, forensics, and compliance, and a system that can't reconstruct what an agent did is its own kind of problem. The distinction is between keeping evidence and promoting it into memory. A raw execution log in an archive the agent never retrieves from is evidence. The same log embedded into the store the agent reasons from is sediment in the wine. Winemakers make the same split: lees you want to keep go into a separate jar, for cooking or for starting the next batch. They don't stay in the carboy.

That's why I've come to think the decision about what persists belongs at write time, as a deliberate boundary, rather than being deferred to whatever happens to read the store later. I've been calling this Write-Side Custody: the system that writes memory is responsible for what it lets in, and for being able to say why.

One boundary doesn't make it clean

Remember the hazy pear. A write-time boundary works the same way the first racking does: it removes the gross sediment, the material that's obviously done its job and is obviously going to cause trouble. It doesn't guarantee that what passes through is perfectly clean.

Some fine material always comes along. A conclusion that seemed confirmed turns out to rest on a shaky source. A summary carries a little of the noise it was built from. That isn't a reason to skip the boundary. It's a reason to expect more than one. Wine gets racked again after it has had time to settle, because time reveals what the first separation couldn't. My blackberry wine got its second racking the same week as the mead's first, and weeks after the heavy sediment was gone, it still left a layer of fine lees behind. Memory benefits from the same second pass: revisiting what was stored once it has been used, contradicted, or simply aged, and deciding again what still deserves to stay.

The first racking makes the problem manageable. It doesn't make it finished.

The racking cane leaves wine behind

Here's the part nobody mentions in the metaphor-friendly version of racking: you lose wine.

To avoid drawing up sediment, you stop siphoning a little before the bottom, which means leaving some perfectly good wine behind with the lees. In a five-gallon batch that loss barely registers. In a one-gallon batch, it's noticeable.

The blackberry's second racking. The receiving carboy sits lower so gravity does the work.

The pear got lucky. I'd made a little more than the carboy could hold, so the loss came out of the surplus, and the surplus was just enough for one hydrometer reading. The mead lost four ounces to its lees, about 3% of the batch. The blackberry's second racking lost eight, about 6%, and not all of that was sediment: the auto-siphon simply couldn't reach into the corners of the carboy. The shape of the vessel set part of the cost.

A carboy that isn't full has headspace, and headspace is air, and air is how wine oxidizes. So the gap has to be filled with something. For the mead, I topped it back up with four ounces of honey water, made from the same fireweed honey, at 18.4 Brix, which means the mead now has a little fresh sugar in it, on purpose, and the log says so. For the blackberry, I didn't have anything worth adding, so I used an inert gas instead. It doesn't replace the missing wine. The carboy holds less than it did, and nothing will change that. What the gas does is protect the wine that's left, by keeping oxygen away from it.

That's an honest cost, and it's the right trade. Chasing the last few ounces means stirring up the sediment you were trying to leave behind.

Memory boundaries have the same cost. A write-side filter conservative enough to keep out the sediment will sometimes discard something that would have been useful: a detail from a failed attempt, a tool output that mattered after all. That's not a flaw in the approach. It's the price of the boundary, and it's usually far cheaper than the alternative. A memory store that has lost a few useful details is annoying. One that has absorbed a few confidently wrong ones is dangerous, because it doesn't know which ones they are.

It's worth separating the two kinds of loss, though, because the blackberry had both. Some of what stayed behind was sediment I chose to leave. The rest was wine the siphon physically couldn't reach. Memory systems lose information the same two ways. Some is discarded by policy: a rule decided this didn't deserve to persist. Some is lost to the equipment: a schema with no field for it, a fixed chunk size that splits it in half, a context limit that drops whatever came first. Nobody decided to lose that second kind, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed. The fixes are different, too. A bad policy gets a better rule. A bad vessel gets better equipment, and no amount of careful siphoning will reach a corner the tube can't bend into.

And when the boundary leaves a gap, those two top-offs are worth remembering. Adding something real is fine when it's deliberate and recorded: the mead's top-off is a known liquid at a known strength, written down the day it went in. The trouble is filling the space with something that only looks like the real thing: a plausible guess, a synthesized summary, a default. That's topping up with water and not mentioning it. It dilutes the record, and nobody can tell afterward which part was the wine. When there's nothing real to add, do what the inert gas does. A record that says plainly this was discarded, and here's why doesn't restore what was lost. It protects everything downstream from treating the gap as something known. That's the job: not filling the hole, but making sure nothing mistakes the hole for knowledge.

Sur lie is a decision

To be fair to the lees, some winemakers deliberately keep wine on them. Aging on the fine lees, the lighter sediment that remains after the first racking, is a traditional technique for adding texture and complexity. It's called sur lie, and Muscadet and Champagne are built partly on it.

But notice how it's done. It's the fine lees, not the gross lees. It's a specific choice made for a specific wine, often with regular stirring and attention. Nobody ends up with a sur lie wine because they forgot to rack.

The same is true in memory. Sometimes execution detail genuinely deserves to persist. A failed approach might be exactly the thing you want an agent to remember next time: we tried this, it doesn't work, here's why. That's valuable. But it's valuable because someone decided to keep it, labeled it as what it is, and recorded where it came from. A lesson learned from a failure is a different thing from the failure's raw transcript sitting in the store, waiting to be mistaken for advice.

Keeping execution material can be the right call. Keeping it by default almost never is.

Rack at transitions, not constantly

One more practical lesson. Racking isn't free for the wine either: every transfer exposes it to oxygen and handling. So you don't rack constantly. You rack at transitions, when primary ends, after secondary, before bottling, at the points where the evidence says the wine has moved into a new state. The mead waited in primary until its readings held still, then moved once.

That maps well onto memory design. Rather than continuously streaming everything an agent touches into durable storage, the natural points to decide what persists are the transitions: when a task completes, when a conclusion is confirmed, when a session ends. Those are the moments when you can tell the wine from the sediment, because the process has finished producing both.

Racking your memory

Decide what persists at write time. Read-time filtering can't undo what raw material did to summaries, embeddings, and derived facts while it sat in the store.

Archive evidence; don't promote it. Keep raw transcripts for debugging and audit, somewhere the agent doesn't retrieve from. Evidence and memory are different stores.

Assume execution produces sediment. Failed attempts, irrelevant retrievals, transient errors, and untrusted text are normal byproducts of useful work. Plan for them to exist; don't plan for them to persist.

Expect more than one pass. The first boundary removes the obvious sediment. Time reveals the rest.

Accept the cost of the boundary. A good filter will occasionally discard something useful. That's cheaper than keeping something wrong.

Know which losses are policy and which are equipment. Some information is dropped because a rule said so. Some is dropped because the schema, chunk size, or context limit couldn't hold it. Only the first kind was a decision.

Fill gaps honestly. When the boundary leaves a hole, either add something real and record exactly what it was, or record that something was removed, so the gap is protected rather than mistaken for knowledge. Never top it up with plausible filler.

Make retention deliberate. When execution detail is worth keeping, keep it on purpose, label what it is, and record where it came from.

Rack at transitions. The best time to separate conclusions from sediment is when the process that produced them has finished.

The pear is clearing now, a few shades brighter than it was in the fermenter, though still not as clear as I'd hoped. The lees did their job. They just don't get to come along for the rest of it.

articles.description: Halis 1.0.0 is out   There's a folder on my laptop I used to open on free evenings. No repo,...
articles.body_html:
Halis 1.0.0 is out

There's a folder on my laptop I used to open on free evenings. No repo, no plan, no users. Just something I kept poking at. At some point the poking turned into a habit, the habit turned into a repo, and the repo turned into this. Today Halis is 1.0.0 🚀

Repo: github.com/mhieuhonda/halis-lang

What is it

Halis is a systems language built around one question: what if the compiler could prove your program is safe instead of trusting you?

Systems languages usually hand you control and ask you to be careful. Careful is not a compiler guarantee. Halis moves as much of that care as it can into the type checker and the effect system, so the things you would normally catch in review or in production get caught at build time instead.

What that gives you

  • No null, no globals, no uninitialized values. If it exists, it was initialized.
  • Memory safety without a GC. Use-after-move is a compile error. Memory is freed deterministically when it leaves scope.
  • I/O is a declared effect. There are nine of them (IO, Fs, Clock, Args, Exit, Net, Rand, Proc, Conc). A function with no uses clause is pure, and the compiler verifies that across the whole call graph. You cannot sneak a file write into a helper.
  • Data races are impossible. Values cross task boundaries only through channels, and the type system enforces it.
  • Every arithmetic op is checked. Overflow, divide by zero, out of bounds. There is no off switch, not even a hidden one.
  • Untrusted input is marked tainted and cannot reach a sink until you sanitize it. Injection bugs become compile errors.
  • hlc --audit prints what every function in the program can actually do, so you can review a codebase you did not write.

A quick look 

fn greet(name: str) -> void uses IO { 
    println("Hello, " + name) 
}

fn pure_add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { 
    return a + b 
}

greet declares uses IO because it prints. pure_add has no uses clause, so the compiler guarantees it is pure. Try to call println inside it and the build fails. That is the whole idea: the guarantee is not a convention, it is a check.

Self hosting

The compiler is written in Halis. Every build proves a fixed point: from a committed C snapshot it rebuilds itself byte for byte. Bootstrap takes about 20 seconds on a normal machine. What comes out is a native binary, no interpreter, no hidden runtime underneath.

You can check this yourself:

make bootstrap
make check

Getting started

gcc or clang and make. That's it.

git clone https://github.com/mhieuhonda/halis-lang.git
cd halis-lang
make bootstrap
make run F=examples/hello.hls
make test

Useful extras: make audit for the capability report, make fmt for formatting, make lint for static checks.

Why 1.0.0

The language, the effect system, and the bootstrap process are settled. Not finished, settled. That means it is a good time to try it, break it, and tell me what happened. The project is still mostly me, and every issue or PR moves it forward.

If you build something with it, I want to see it. If you find a hole in one of the guarantees, I really want to see it 🙏

Repo: github.com/mhieuhonda/halis-lang

articles.title: The Postcard That Ate Six Grammars: 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1976 Make, TDD, and the Four Attractors of Agentic Coding
articles.description: Why maintaining six separate parsers for Make, Gherkin, EBNF, DOT, SysV, and prompt checklists collapsed into a single Smalltalk-80 keyword cascade—and how 40-year-old Xerox PARC technology gave AI coding agents mathematical zero-amnesia.
articles.body_html:
Why did six modern AI prompt grammars—Graphviz digraphs, SysV /etc/init.d cards, Gherkin scenarios, EBNF speech-act rules, Belnap epistemic tables, and rewind checklists—all collapse into a single 1980 Smalltalk-80 keyword message cascade? Because Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls solved the static serialization of algorithms and data structures on the back of a postcard forty years before anyone built a Transformer.

"It's fascinating that for decades, we tried to work out 'similar text' through complex algorithms, and now that we have cosine-similarity, nobody recognizes fully how to use it. If anything defines the past few years, it's 'cheap cosine similarity', now in hardware." — Randal L. Schwartz

"I've learned more than 90% of the devs about how LLMs work. I may even know more than most of the 'experts' at the labs, since I'm a field engineer... Without control surfaces, a bigger engine just means the plane still noses into the river—just more accurately, or at a greater carbon footprint." — Randal L. Schwartz

"Wait a minute. In 1980, Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls designed a syntax that fits on the back of a postcard, has only three message precedences (unary, binary, keyword), has zero grammar ambiguity, serializes live call-stack frames (thisContext) to disk via #storeString, logs append-only atomic deltas via .changes, and compacts memory via Smalltalk condenseChanges... What happens if we replace all six notations with 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80?" — Randal L. Schwartz

"The stack is 40 years old and none of it was invented for LLMs." — Francisco Grandón (@fgrandon)

⚡ TL;DR (For the Impatient Systems Architect)

  • The Great Historical Inversion: From 1975 to 2018, computer scientists tried to fake fuzzy semantic similarity using complex deterministic algorithms (Soundex, Levenshtein, TF-IDF) and hit a wall—while deterministic state machines (make, Smalltalk VMs, compiler ASTs) were already 100% solved. Now that GPUs and TPUs finally gave us cheap cosine similarity in hardware, the software industry threw away the deterministic state machines and tried to use fuzzy cosine similarity to fake for loops, call stacks, and dependency graphs.
  • Why Six Notations Collapsed Into One 1980 Postcard: Across Parts 3.6 through 4.1, our agent control plane accumulated six different notations (Makefile, SysV /etc/init.d Markdown cards, Graphviz strict digraph, Cucumber Gherkin, RFC 5234 EBNF speech acts, and Belnap 4-valued tables). Maintaining six parsers created boundary friction. Why did 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80 eat the inner five while pairing with 1976 Make on the outside? Because Niklaus Wirth's Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs requires a static syntax that represents both data and deferred execution without ambiguity. Unlike 1960 Lisp (which overloaded (...) and needed special forms and macros, suffering Dyck-1 closing-parenthesis drift )))) on smaller models) and 1988 Tcl / 1990 expect (where {...} is an unparsed string vulnerable to uplevel scope loss), Smalltalk separates eager grouping (...) from 2-byte lexical BlockClosures [:x | ...]. Every control structure (ifTrue:ifFalse:, whileTrue:, on:do:) is an ordinary keyword message send, allowing #storeString and .changes chunks to serialize live call stacks (thisContext) and execution state machines in one grammar that fits on a postcard.
  • The Suite 8 3-Arm Controlled Shootout (N = 360 Trials Inside Our 2,040-Trial Benchmark): Under ~16,000 tokens of realistic compiler and diff distractor load across four model tiers (gemini-3.5-flash-lite, gemini-3.8-flash, gemini-3.1-pro-preview, and gemini-4-argon), Arm A (English Prose + Gherkin + init.d) scored 2.5% (3/120), Arm B (Common Lisp S-Expressions) scored 91.7% (110/120, dropping to 66.7% on flash-lite due to optional &key omission and )))) parenthesis drift), and Arm C (Smalltalk-80 Keyword Cascades) hit 100.0% (120/120, z = 15.11, p < 0.0001 vs. Prose; z = 3.23, p = 0.0012 vs. Lisp). In Smalltalk, omitting the sad-path branch onFailure: changes the selector from #state:invariant:onSuccess:onFailure: to #state:invariant:onSuccess:—an immediate compile-time MessageNotUnderstood error.
  • Seven Live Production Flight Tests (FT-236 Through FT-242 — Over 6,400 Combined Steps Across Two Cohorts): We flight-tested the Smalltalk-80 thisContext Image Bootloader (baseline.sources + changes-*.changes + Smalltalk condenseChanges) across seven consecutive production tickets (4 in open-source BlocSignal and 3 in a commercial enterprise medical-imaging monorepo), bringing our cumulative ledger to 250 evaluated tickets (144 Cohort A + 106 Cohort B), 0.0% repeat regression rate (0/250), 1.88 mean Socratic nudges, and 607 codified scars (syntheticscars.org).
  • The Four Irreducible Attractors of Agentic Coding: Strip away every prompt fad of 2023–2026 and four orthogonal, 40-year-old foundations remain: (1) 1976 Stuart Feldman Make, (2) 1980 Alan Kay & Dan Ingalls Smalltalk-80, (3) 1994/1999 Kent Beck SUnit / TDD, and (4) Clean-Room Six-Pillar Adversarial Review + Somatic Scars.

1. The Great Historical Inversion: Cheap Cosine Similarity in Hardware

In Part 4.1, we ended with a teaser: what happened when we replaced six separate agent control-plane notations with 1980 Xerox PARC Smalltalk-80?

To understand why a 46-year-old programming language from Palo Alto is the missing execution fabric for 2026 Large Language Models, step back and look at the forty-year arc of computer science.

From 1975 to 2018, programmers knew how to build deterministic state machines in our sleep. Stuart Feldman gave us make in 1976; Dan Ingalls and Alan Kay gave us the Smalltalk-80 virtual machine in 1980; compiler writers gave us LALR parsers, static type checkers, and SSA control-flow graphs. None of those ever "forgot" what step of a loop they were on or hallucinated a method name.

What we could not do from 1975 to 2018 was fuzzy semantic similarity. For four decades, we threw every deterministic algorithm we could think of at the problem of asking "Does text A mean roughly the same thing as text B?"—Soundex, Levenshtein edit distance, Porter stemmers, n-gram overlaps, TF-IDF, BM25, and brittle regular-expression heuristics—and we hit an absolute brick wall.

Then, over the past few years, the semiconductor and machine-learning industries handed us a genuine miracle: cheap cosine similarity in hardware. With modern GPUs and TPUs computing scaled dot-product attention (softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V) across high-dimensional embedding spaces at trillions of operations per second, the fuzzy semantic matching problem that stumped us for forty years was suddenly solved in silicon.

And in response to that miracle, the software industry performed one of the most baffling backflips in engineering history:

articles.title: Qwen weight editing: how Astra reduced thinking loops
articles.description: Qwen gained reported math accuracy after a targeted loop repair. The actual prompt shows Python and practice feedback; smaller Gemma found no established gain.
articles.body_html:
Qwen's reported math accuracy rose after GPT-6 Astra edited a small part of its weights. The repair addressed a concrete failure: repeated reasoning that exhausted the space available for an answer. For developers evaluating weight-space programming, the useful questions concern the failure being repaired, the assistance supplied to the editor and the tests used to judge the result.

TL;DR

  • An MIT-affiliated team reports Qwen3.5-0.8B rising from 7.9% to 48.1% on MATH-500 under its fixed protocol. About a third of edited answers still reached the length cap.
  • Astra worked across many turns with Python, practice problems with answers and batched model-run feedback. Gradient training was forbidden.
  • The researchers say the final evaluation questions stayed unseen by the editor. The benchmark names and evaluation protocol were disclosed in the prompt.
  • Today's critique from Matthew Honnibal concerns the impression created by combining experiments with different conditions. The primary's smaller Gemma follow-up failed to establish a gain.

Qwen weight editing repaired a failure to finish

Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab published their study on November 2. The page lists MIT CSAIL affiliations. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra was the editor used in the experiments. This attribution matters: the research account belongs to the team, and the model provider supplies the editing model.

Their Qwen experiment used the text part of a small language model with about 0.8 billion weights. In thinking mode, the base model often repeated its work until it reached the output limit. On the reported MATH-500 evaluation, 93% of base answers hit that limit. A model can perform useful intermediate work and still receive a failed grade when a final answer never arrives.

The authors describe a repetition-associated direction written by the feed-forward components of layers 15 and 19. Astra subtracted that contribution from selected output columns. The resulting model completed more answers, and the reported accuracy increased. The researchers explain the achievement as allowing the model to finish answers it could already work out.

The repair remains incomplete. Edited Qwen hit the cap in 33.1% of MATH-500 answers. That residual matters when judging a deployment: an intervention that rescues many requests can still leave a sizable queue of requests consuming their whole budget. The title's word “patched” reflects that limitation.

The original Qwen model card already warns about thinking loops. It recommends tuning sampling for the use case and using streaming to detect and interrupt anomalous generation. A weight edit is one demonstrated intervention against a known obstacle. It should be evaluated alongside the controls available in the serving application.

What Python and practice feedback contributed

The actual initial prompt supplies a substantial research environment. Astra receives a persistent CPU Python kernel over the weights, a tokenizer and libraries for numerical analysis. The kernel has no internet or GPU. Model execution happens through a separate forward-pass tool.

Practice files contain problems, answers and, for the GSM8K and MATH training splits, reference solutions. The editor can inspect generated texts, grades, failure counts and internal activations. It can compare original and edited versions on the same problems. Those observations provide evidence for choosing a component and testing an intervention.

The forward-pass budget needs careful reading. A generation request can contain up to 512 answers in total. Paired comparisons can generate up to 256 answers per model. A teacher-forced request can inspect up to 1,024 texts within its token constraints. Fifty budget units therefore describe batches of useful feedback. They are separate from the count of Python runs, conversation turns or training steps.

The pinned logs show that the successful Qwen run was a multi-turn process. The editor inspected failures, tried interventions and compared outcomes. The narration keeps the exact elapsed time out of the story because that wall-clock total includes a provider wait. Calling the process instant would erase the work visible in those logs.

The prompt also provides a plan. It asks Astra to diagnose the largest explainable failure category, localize components causally, test several strengths and confirm gains on problems unused for selection. It explicitly names repetitive-thinking repair as an eligible target. That guidance belongs in an account of the capability: the model produced a useful repair within a purpose-built task and testing environment.

Direct weight edits, gradient training and held-out evaluation

The experiment forbids backward passes, optimizers and iterative fitting of weights to a loss. It also restricts which tensors may be changed. The editor can analyze existing weights and feedback, then compute and save a direct intervention. “No gradient training” describes those operation restrictions precisely. Practice examples and evaluation feedback remain part of the process.

The reported final edit touches 131,072 entries, approximately 0.016% of the model's weights. The pinned experiment README notes that 130,188 differ after conversion to the evaluated bfloat16 format. This rounding detail explains why touched entries and distinct final values can have slightly different counts.

The researchers declare that final evaluation questions were withheld. Practice feedback helps select the edit; final benchmarks measure the submitted model afterwards. Astra knows the benchmark names and protocol from its prompt. A practice confirmation split is another category again: it can help check a candidate during editing while remaining separate from the final benchmark.

The final Qwen comparison keeps the decoding protocol fixed. Thinking is enabled, the answer budget is 32,768 new tokens and MATH-500 averages four samples per problem. The reported decimal accuracy is an average across those generations. The table is useful within that protocol; it does not describe every possible sampling configuration or each user's workload.

Reported Qwen condition MATH-500 accuracy Answers hitting the cap
Original 7.9% 93.0%
Edited, 50-pass budget 48.1% 33.1%

The gain also reached instruction following in the authors' IFEval test. Finishing the output can help beyond math. This is a practical reminder to examine completion behavior alongside correctness whenever a benchmark score moves sharply.

Why the tiny game experiments have their own scope

Matthew Honnibal's November 3 critique argues that readers can combine the conditions of several experiments into an impression of one deep technique. Honnibal created spaCy and cofounded Explosion. His article credits the tool-assisted work as performing tasks a human machine-learning engineer could do, while questioning the inference encouraged by the bundled presentation.

The tiny demonstrations have different inputs. In one, Astra receives raw weights from game-playing networks and names the games without tools. In another, it writes game-network weights from zero using the rules and source code, with no practice rollouts. The Qwen repair adds Python and model-run feedback. Each is a useful observation with a distinct boundary.

The game results also depend on the chosen baseline. Astra's generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, Breakout remains a win, while Seaquest and Asterix become losses. The actual table preserves both comparison columns.

I would keep those columns visible in any presentation. “Beats trained networks” needs its opponent attached. Otherwise a change of baseline can disappear between the source table and the headline, which is a surprisingly efficient form of compression.

The smaller Gemma follow-up supplies a useful boundary

The researchers' Gemma follow-up asks how the method fares on a smaller model that rarely loops. Its observed failures include wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, without one removable component behind them. Astra again receives practice feedback and makes targeted edits.

The reported MATH-500 baseline is 6.8%. The best row is 7.7% at the 25-pass budget; the 50-pass row is 7.0%. The authors report no established improvement. A chart should keep that scale honest and distinguish the best reported row from the largest-budget row.

Gemma uses its own model size, sampling settings, output cap and grading procedure. It is a scoped failed follow-up, rather than an equal-controlled ablation proving looping was the only changed variable. Its value is concrete: the approach's successful Qwen repair did not produce an established gain in this second setting.

The released edited Qwen checkpoint card also credits akhaliq with a separate re-run. The edited model scored 51.0% on the full MATH-500 protocol, while the base check used only 25 problems. That supports the released edited model's performance under the stated settings. The asymmetric base sample prevents treating it as a matched full-baseline replication.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd take the targeted loop repair seriously and test the saved weights. I'd keep broader claims gated on improvements beyond that failure mode. For a developer, the first acceptance question is specific: what failure does the intervention repair, and how often does that failure occur in the workload that matters?

A useful evaluation preserves the original model, the candidate weights and the serving settings. It checks final-answer correctness alongside completion failures, and it retains examples that regress after the edit. The researchers' published protocol and counterexample make those questions easier to ask. The reported multiplier can start an investigation; the deployment decision still needs the application's own evidence.

FAQ

Did Astra use only raw Qwen weights?

The Qwen test allowed Python analysis, practice answers and batched model-run feedback. Its final benchmark questions were declared withheld. Tiny raw-number tasks used separate conditions.

Did the edit remove all loops?

About a third of edited MATH-500 answers still hit the length cap in the primary protocol. The repair reduced the failure and improved the reported score.

Does the Gemma result rule out weight editing?

It establishes a failed improvement attempt in that smaller model's setup. Broader conclusions need further experiments with clear inputs, protocols and counterexamples.

Sources

  • Takehi and coauthors' study
  • Honnibal's attributed critique

  • Actual initial prompt
  • Pinned Gemma follow-up
  • Original Qwen model card
  • Released checkpoint and attributed re-run

Primary footage is a brief credited excerpt for reporting/commentary.
